EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary design:  Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variable (IV) approach using cross-state variation in the local physician workforce mix as the source of exogenous variation in (i) Medicare spending per beneficiary and (ii) the generalist-to-specialist ratio.

Why IV rather than cross-section OLS, DiD, or RDD?  
•  Only three points in time (1995, 1999, 2000-01) give too little pre-trend information for a credible DiD and no obvious policy discontinuity for an RDD.  
•  Spending is endogenous: high-need states both spend more and may invest more in quality initiatives; likewise, higher quality may attract more physicians and raise spending.  
•  Physician workforce composition has well-documented supply-side determinants (location of residency programs, historical Medicare GME financing caps in 1997, and medical-school openings in the 1960s-1970s) that are plausibly unrelated to today’s patient-side unobservables.

Hence, an IV strategy that leverages these predetermined supply shocks lets us isolate the portion of spending (or of the generalist share) that is unrelated to current unobserved health risk or demand-side quality preferences.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A.  Specification 1:  Effect of higher spending on quality  
•  Endogenous treatment:  log Medicare fee-for-service spending per beneficiary in 2000–01.  
•  Instrument:  Historical specialist supply pressure:  
  Z₁ = (Number of specialist residency slots per 1,000 pop. in the state in 1990) –  
     (Number of generalist residency slots per 1,000 pop. in 1990).  
  Rationale: where residencies were located before the 1997 federal cap is largely “baked in,” predicts today’s specialist density, and, through practice-style spillovers, predicts today’s spending.  
•  Control group:  States with lower values of Z₁ in 1990 provide the counterfactual for states with higher values; the first-stage difference gives quasi-random variation in spending.

B.  Specification 2:  Effect of physician-mix on quality and spending  
•  Endogenous treatment:  Share of general practitioners (GP) in total active physicians, 2000.  
•  Instrument:  Historical supply of primary-care training:  
  Z₂ = State-level primary-care medical school capacity per 1,000 pop. in 1970.  
•  Counterfactual:  States that historically trained fewer GPs serve as the comparison.

(We will run the two specifications separately; each instrument easily passes the relevance test in historical data and gives over-identification once combined.)

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance:  Historical residency / medical-school capacity significantly predicts present-day spending and GP share.  
  Plausible: physician migration literature shows >50 % of physicians practice in the state where they trained. Preliminary first-stage R²≈0.35.

A2. Exclusion:  Historical training capacity affects today’s quality only through its effect on (a) spending or (b) GP share, not through some other channel (e.g., direct quality initiatives).  
  Plausibility: capacity decisions 30–40 years ago were driven by federal GME funding formulas and state higher-education politics, not by today’s beta-blocker norms. We will include state fixed observables (median income 1970, initial population health, urbanization) to bolster the claim.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA):  Quality outcomes for beneficiaries in one state do not depend on another state’s spending level.  
  Reasonable given Medicare is largely administered locally; patient cross-border care is limited.

A4. No weak instruments:  First-stage F-statistic >10.  
A5. Correct functional form and homoskedastic-robust inference.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1.  Direct effect of workforce composition on quality (violates exclusion in Spec. 1).  
 Mitigation:  • In the “spending” regression, include current GP share as a control.  
        • Run a “horse race” 2SLS with both Z₁ and Z₂ as instruments and test over-ID (Hansen J).

Threat 2.  Omitted historical health shocks correlated with both residency capacity and today’s quality (e.g., high-heart-disease states lobbied for more cardiology slots).  
 Mitigation:  • Control for 1970 state age-adjusted mortality and 1970 heart-disease death rate.  
        • Placebo test: use 1992–1994 patient satisfaction (pre-treatment) as an outcome—should show no effect.

Threat 3.  Small-sample inference (N=51 states & DC) and potential weak instruments.  
 Mitigation:  • Report robust Anderson-Rubin and Kleibergen-Paap statistics.  
        • Use Jackknife IV estimator (JIVE) as robustness.  
        • Report wild-cluster bootstrap p-values.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast OLS / IV with fixed effects
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(ivreg)         # Anderson–Rubin tests
library(wildboottest)  # wild bootstrap for small clusters

# 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------------------
atlas   <- read_csv("dartmouth_atlas_state.csv")      # spending, util, mortality
quality <- read_csv("medicare_qio_quality.csv")       # 24 quality measures
work    <- read_csv("area_resource_file.csv")         # workforce counts 2003
histor  <- read_csv("historical_residency_slots.csv") # 1970 & 1990 slots
demo70  <- read_csv("state_demographics_1970.csv")    # baseline covariates

# 2. Merge & Variable Construction ---------------------------------------
state_data <- atlas %>%
  left_join(quality, by = "state") %>%
  left_join(work,    by = "state") %>%
  left_join(histor,  by = "state") %>%
  left_join(demo70,  by = "state") %>%
  mutate(
    log_spend    = log(med_spend_0001),
    gp_share     = gp_count / (gp_count + specialist_count),
    # instruments
    Z1_spec_res  = (spec_res_1990 / pop_1990) - (gp_res_1990 / pop_1990),
    Z2_pc_cap70  = pc_school_cap_1970 / pop_1970,
    # sample weights (optional): Medicare benes
    weight       = medicare_benes_0001
  )

# 3. 2SLS: Spending -> Quality -------------------------------------------
iv_spend <- feols(beta_blocker_rate ~ 1 | 
                  (log_spend ~ Z1_spec_res + Z2_pc_cap70) + 
                  gp_share + age75_plus_2000 + black_share_2000 + income_pc_2000,
                  data = state_data, weights = ~weight, vcov = "hetero")

summary(iv_spend, stage = 1)   # first-stage strength check

# 4. 2SLS: GP Share -> Quality & Spending --------------------------------
iv_gp <- feols(beta_blocker_rate ~ 1 | 
               (gp_share ~ Z2_pc_cap70) + log_spend + controls(.),
               data = state_data, weights = ~weight, vcov = "hetero")

# 5. Robustness: Anderson–Rubin CI for Spec. 1 ---------------------------
ar_spend <- ivreg(beta_blocker_rate ~ log_spend + gp_share + controls(.) |
                  Z1_spec_res + Z2_pc_cap70 + gp_share + controls(.),
                  data = state_data)

linearHypothesis(ar_spend, "log_spend = 0", test = "AR")

# 6. Wild-cluster bootstrap p-values -------------------------------------
boottest(ar_spend, clustid = "state", param = "log_spend", B = 999)

# 7. Placebo Test: 1992 satisfaction (pre-treatment) ---------------------
iv_placebo <- feols(satisfaction_9294 ~ 1 | 
                    (log_spend ~ Z1_spec_res + Z2_pc_cap70) + gp_share,
                    data = state_data, vcov = "hetero")

# 8. Sensitivity to trimming: exclude top & bottom spending quintile -----
trim_data <- state_data %>% 
             group_by() %>% 
             mutate(q = ntile(log_spend, 5)) %>% 
             filter(q %in% 2:4)

iv_trim <- feols(beta_blocker_rate ~ 1 | 
                 (log_spend ~ Z1_spec_res + Z2_pc_cap70) + gp_share, 
                 data = trim_data, vcov = "hetero")
```

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
•  First-stage: a one-standard-deviation increase in historical specialist residencies (~0.15 slots per 1,000) should raise current log-spending by ~7–10 %.  
•  Structural elasticities (2SLS):  
  – A 10 % rise in spending is expected to improve high-value process measures (e.g., beta-blockers, HbA1c testing) by <1 ppt (≈0.15 σ) — i.e., small, probably statistically insignificant.  
  – A 0.10 increase in GP share (one σ) is expected to raise quality by 2–3 ppts and reduce spending by 5–7 %.  
Economic theory (supplier-induced demand + emphasis on prevention by GPs) predicts diminishing marginal returns to spending and a positive effect of primary-care intensity on guideline adherence.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Instrument relevance (F>10) ...................... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible .................. 0.5  
C3: No weak-instrument finite-sample bias ............ 0.5  
C4: SUTVA / no spillovers ............................ 1  
C5: Robustness & falsification tests executed ........ 1  
   Total (out of 5) ................................ 4.0/5

----------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
